title: Not to communicate a man's honour
paragraphs: Of all the follies of the world, the one most universally embraced is concern for reputation and glory; we are so fond of it that we abandon riches, peace, life, and health — which are real and substantial goods — to chase after this empty phantom of a word, with no body to it, no hold to take on it:
"La fama, ch'invaghisce a un dolce suono Gli superbi mortali, et par si bella, E un eco, un sogno, anzi d'un sogno un'ombra, Ch'ad ogni vento si dilegua a sgombra."

["Fame, which with sweet sound charms proud mortals and seems so fair, is but an echo, a dream — nay, the shadow of a dream — which at every breath of wind vanishes and dissolves." — Tasso, Gerus., xiv. 63.]

And of all the irrational humours of men, it would seem that the philosophers themselves are among the last and most reluctant to free themselves from this one; it's the most stubborn and obstinate of all:
"Quia etiam bene proficientes animos tentare non cessat."
["Because it does not cease to assail even well-directed minds." — St. Augustine, De Civit. Dei, v. 14.]

There is no folly whose vanity reason exposes more clearly; but it is so deeply rooted in us that I don't dare decide whether anyone has ever wholly cleared themselves of it. Even after you have said all and believed all that can be said against it, it produces such an inward inclination in opposition to your best arguments that you have little power to resist it. As Cicero says, even those who most argue against it would yet have the books they write on the subject appear under their own names, and seek to derive glory from seeming to despise it. Everything else is communicable and enters into commerce: we lend our goods and stake our lives for the needs and service of our friends; but to share one's honour, and dress another man in one's own glory, is very rarely seen.

And yet we have some examples of just that. Catulus Luctatius in the Cimbrian war, having done all he could to make his fleeing soldiers turn and face the enemy, finally fled with them himself, faking the coward, so that his men would look as though they were following their captain rather than running from the enemy — sacrificing his own reputation in order to cover the shame of others. When Charles V came into Provence in 1537, it is said that Antonio de Leva, seeing the emperor firmly resolved on the expedition and believing it would do him great honour, nevertheless very stiffly opposed it in council, so that the entire glory of the resolution would be attributed to his master, and it could be said his own wisdom and foresight were such that, against everyone else's opinion, he had brought about so great an enterprise — which was to do him honour at his own expense. The Thracian ambassadors, coming to console Archileonida, the mother of Brasidas, on the death of her son, and praising him to the point of saying he had left no equal behind him, she rejected this private and particular praise to attribute it to the public: "Don't tell me that," she said. "I know the city of Sparta has many citizens both greater and of greater worth than he." In the battle of Crécy, the Prince of Wales, then very young, had been given command of the vanguard; the brunt of the battle happened to fall in that part of the field, which led the lords with him, finding themselves overmatched, to send to King Edward to come up to their relief. He asked how his son was, and being told he was alive and on horseback: "Then I'd do him wrong," said the king, "to go and rob him of the honour of winning this battle he has sustained so long and so bravely. Whatever risk he runs, the honour shall be entirely his own." And accordingly he would neither come up himself nor send help, knowing that if he went, it would be said all would have been lost without his rescue, and the honour of the victory would be wholly given to him.
"Semper enim quod postremum adjectum est, id rem totam videtur traxisse."
["For that which is last added always seems to have accomplished the whole affair." — Livy, xxvii. 45.]

Many at Rome thought, and often said, that the greatest of Scipio's deeds were in part due to Laelius, whose constant practice it was always to advance and uphold Scipio's grandeur and renown without any care for his own. And Theopompus, king of Sparta, said to a man who told him the republic couldn't fail because he himself knew so well how to command: "It's rather," he replied, "because the people know so well how to obey." Just as women who succeeded to peerages had, despite their sex, the privilege of attending and voting in trials within the jurisdiction of the peers, so the ecclesiastical peers, despite their profession, were obliged to attend our kings in their wars, not just with their friends and servants but in person. The Bishop of Beauvais did so when he was with Philip Augustus at the battle of Bouvines, where he played a notable part in the action; but he didn't think it fitting for him to share in the fruit and glory of that violent and bloody trade. He took several of the enemy that day with his own hand and turned them over to the first gentleman he met, leaving it to him either to kill them or to accept their surrender, referring the whole execution to that other hand. He did this with the Earl of Salisbury, William, whom he handed over to Messire Jehan de Nesle. By a similar subtlety of conscience to the one I have just mentioned, he would kill but not wound, and so always fought with a mace. And a certain person of my own time, being reproached by the king for having laid hands on a priest, flatly and positively denied any such thing — meaning he had cudgelled and kicked him.
